## Topics covered

-   Confidence intervals for a mean and for a proportion
-   The meaning of the confidence level
-   Significance tests for a proportion and for a mean
-   Comparing the means of two groups

::: callout-note
#### Note

The exercises associated with this unit are available at
[this link](https://tommasorigon.github.io/EnvEcoStat/exe/exe_C.html).
:::

## Horseshoe crabs

A study considered $n = 173$ female [horseshoe crabs]{.orange} on an island off
the coast of Florida. During the spawning season, a female migrates to the
shore with a male attached to her, and lays her eggs in the sand.

Other males, called [satellites]{.blue}, may cluster around the pair and also
fertilise the eggs. For each female, the data report:

-   `width`, the width of the carapace (cm);
-   `y`, equal to $1$ if the female has at least one satellite, $0$ otherwise.

::: callout-note
#### Research question

How large are female horseshoe crabs? Do larger females attract more males?
:::

The data are on the [website of the book](https://stat4ds.rwth-aachen.de/data/):

```{r}
path <- "https://stat4ds.rwth-aachen.de/data/Crabs.dat"
Crabs <- read.table(path, header = TRUE)
str(Crabs)
```

## A confidence interval for the mean

The standard deviation $\sigma$ of the population is unknown. A
$100(1-\alpha)\%$ confidence interval for the mean width $\mu$ is $$
\left(\bar{y} - t_{\alpha/2,\,n-1} \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}, \ \bar{y} + t_{\alpha/2,\,n-1} \frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}\right),
$$ where $t_{\alpha/2,\,n-1}$ is the quantile of the $t$ distribution with
$n - 1$ degrees of freedom and [right-tail]{.orange} probability $\alpha/2$:

```{r}
y <- Crabs$width
n <- length(y)
alpha <- 0.05 # 95% confidence level
t_quant <- qt(1 - alpha / 2, df = n - 1) # Right-tail probability alpha / 2

c(mean(y) - t_quant * sd(y) / sqrt(n), mean(y) + t_quant * sd(y) / sqrt(n))
```

The command `t.test` computes the same interval, reported in its output as
`95 percent confidence interval`:

```{r}
t.test(y, conf.level = 0.95)
```

Since $n \ge 30$, using the normal quantile $z_{1-\alpha/2}$ would give almost
the same result: compare `qnorm(0.975)` and `qt(0.975, df = 172)`.

## A confidence interval for a proportion

The proportion of females with at least one satellite is the mean of the
variable `y`. If $n\hat{\pi} \ge 10$ and $n(1-\hat{\pi}) \ge 10$, a
$100(1-\alpha)\%$ confidence interval for $\pi$ is $$
\left(\hat{\pi} - z_{1-\alpha/2}\sqrt{\frac{\hat{\pi}(1-\hat{\pi})}{n}}, \ \hat{\pi} + z_{1-\alpha/2}\sqrt{\frac{\hat{\pi}(1-\hat{\pi})}{n}}\right).
$$

```{r}
pi_hat <- mean(Crabs$y) # Sample proportion
c(n * pi_hat, n * (1 - pi_hat)) # Both larger than 10

z_quant <- qnorm(1 - alpha / 2)
se_hat <- sqrt(pi_hat * (1 - pi_hat) / n) # Estimated standard error
c(pi_hat - z_quant * se_hat, pi_hat + z_quant * se_hat)
```

::: callout-note
#### Note

The command `prop.test` computes a slightly different (and more accurate)
interval, which is why here we use the formula directly.
:::

## What does 95% confidence mean?

Let us go back to the PM2.5 campaign of [Unit I](un_I.html), where we know that
$\mu = 28$. We simulate $R = 1000$ campaigns of $64$ days and, for each of them,
we check whether the $95\%$ confidence interval [contains]{.orange} $\mu$. With
`$conf.int` we extract only the interval from the output of `t.test`, as we do
with the columns of a data frame:

```{r}
mu <- 28
sigma <- 12
k <- mu^2 / sigma^2
lambda <- mu / sigma^2

set.seed(123)
R <- 1000
covers <- rep(NA, R)

for (r in 1:R) {
  y_sim <- rgamma(64, shape = k, rate = lambda) # A new campaign
  ci <- t.test(y_sim)$conf.int # Its 95% confidence interval
  covers[r] <- (ci[1] < mu) & (mu < ci[2]) # TRUE if the interval contains mu
}

mean(covers) # Proportion of intervals that contain mu
```

About $95\%$ of the intervals contain $\mu$. The confidence level is a property
of the [procedure]{.blue}: a single interval either contains $\mu$ or not.

## A test for a proportion

Let us go back to the [survey on climate change]{.orange} of
[Unit I](un_I.html): $524$ people out of $1008$ said that climate change is a
major threat. We test $$
H_0: \pi = 0.5, \qquad H_a: \pi \neq 0.5.
$$

Under $H_0$, the test statistic $$
z = \frac{\hat{\pi} - \pi_0}{\sqrt{\pi_0(1-\pi_0)/n}}
$$ has approximately a standard normal distribution. The two-sided
[P-value]{.blue} is $\mathbb{P}(|Z| \ge |z|) = 2\,\mathbb{P}(Z \ge |z|)$:

```{r}
pi_hat <- 524 / 1008
pi_0 <- 0.5
z <- (pi_hat - pi_0) / sqrt(pi_0 * (1 - pi_0) / 1008) # Observed test statistic
z
2 * (1 - pnorm(abs(z))) # Two-sided P-value
```

The P-value is larger than $\alpha = 0.05$: we [do not reject]{.orange} $H_0$,
as we guessed in Unit I through simulation. The command `prop.test` gives the
same P-value:

```{r}
prop.test(524, 1008, p = 0.5, correct = FALSE)
```

## A test for a mean

A study compared therapies for $72$ young girls suffering from
[anorexia]{.orange}. For each girl, the weight (in pounds) is measured before and
after the therapy. Let us consider the $29$ girls who received the cognitive
behavioural therapy (`cb`):

```{r}
path <- "https://stat4ds.rwth-aachen.de/data/Anorexia.dat"
Anorexia <- read.table(path, header = TRUE)
change <- Anorexia$after - Anorexia$before # Weight change
change_cb <- change[Anorexia$therapy == "cb"] # Cognitive behavioural therapy
```

Does the therapy change the weight, on average? We test
$H_0: \mu = 0$ against $H_a: \mu \neq 0$. Under $H_0$, the test statistic
$$
t = \frac{\bar{y} - \mu_0}{s / \sqrt{n}}
$$ has a $t$ distribution with $n - 1$ degrees of freedom:

```{r}
n <- length(change_cb)
t_obs <- (mean(change_cb) - 0) / (sd(change_cb) / sqrt(n)) # Observed test statistic
2 * (1 - pt(abs(t_obs), df = n - 1)) # Two-sided P-value
```

```{r}
t.test(change_cb, mu = 0)
```

The P-value is smaller than $0.05$: we [reject]{.orange} $H_0$. Coherently, the
$95\%$ confidence interval does not contain $0$.

## Comparing two groups

Back to the horseshoe crabs: do females with satellites ($y = 1$) have a larger
carapace than those without ($y = 0$)?

```{r}
boxplot(width ~ y, data = Crabs, xlab = "Satellites (0 = no, 1 = yes)", ylab = "Width (cm)")
```

The command `t.test` with a [formula]{.blue} compares the means of the two
groups, testing $H_0: \mu_0 = \mu_1$ and giving a confidence interval for the
difference $\mu_0 - \mu_1$:

```{r}
t.test(width ~ y, data = Crabs, var.equal = TRUE)
```

The P-value is very small: females with satellites are, on average,
[larger]{.orange}.

::: callout-note
#### Note

The option `var.equal = TRUE` assumes that the two groups have the same
variability. By default, **R** uses a version of the test that does not make
this assumption.
:::
